questions.question: Which of the following is an ore of mercury?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cinnabar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cinnabar** is the primary and most common ore of **mercury (Hg)**.
 
• Chemically, it is known as **Mercury(II) sulfide** and its chemical formula is **HgS**.
 
• It typically appears as a **bright red** or **brownish-red** crystalline solid, which has been historically used as a **pigment** known as **vermilion**.
 
• The extraction of mercury from cinnabar involves **roasting** the ore in a furnace. During this process, **sulfur** in the ore combines with **oxygen** to form sulfur dioxide, and the mercury **vaporizes**.
 
• The mercury vapor is then **cooled** and **condensed** to collect **liquid mercury**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Bauxite**:

 
 
• It is the principal ore of **Aluminium (Al)**.
 
• It is not a specific mineral but a **sedimentary rock** with high aluminum content, primarily consisting of **gibbsite**, **boehmite**, and **diaspore**.
 
• **Australia** is the world's largest producer of bauxite, while in **India**, the state of **Odisha** is the leading producer.
 
 
 
• **Magnetite**:
 
 
• It is one of the most important ores of **Iron (Fe)**.
 
• Its chemical formula is **Fe3O4** and it is known for its **natural magnetic** properties, often called **lodestone**.
 
• It has a very high iron content, approximately **72.4%**, making it a high-quality ore.
 
 
 
• **Malachite**:
 
 
• It is a **copper carbonate hydroxide** mineral with the formula **Cu2CO3(OH)2**.
 
• It is a minor ore of **Copper (Cu)** and is easily recognizable by its distinct **bright green** color.
 
• It was often used as a **mineral pigment** in green paints in ancient times.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mercury (Hg)**: It is also known as **quicksilver** and is the only common metal that is **liquid** at standard temperature and pressure.
 
• **Applications**: Due to its uniform **thermal expansion**, mercury is used in **thermometers**, **barometers**, and **manometers**. It is also used in **fluorescent lighting** and **dental amalgams**.
 
• **Amalgams**: Mercury can dissolve many other metals (like gold and silver) to form alloys called **amalgams**. However, it does not form amalgams with **iron**, which is why it is often stored in **iron flasks**.
 
• **Toxicity**: Mercury is highly **toxic** to humans. **Minamata disease** is a neurological syndrome caused by severe **mercury poisoning**, famously occurring in **Japan** in the **1950s**.

questions.question: The Durgapur steel plant was set up in collaboration with the government of the ____.
questions.solution:
p- The correct answer is __**United Kingdom**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Durgapur Steel Plant (DSP)** is one of the integrated steel plants of **Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL)**, located in **Durgapur**, in the **Paschim Bardhaman** district of **West Bengal**.
 
• It was set up in the late **1950s** with the help of a consortium of **British** companies known as **ISCON** (Indian Steelworks Construction Co. Ltd.).
 
• The establishment of this plant was a major part of the **Second Five Year Plan** (**1956-1961**), which focused on the development of heavy industries and capital goods in India.
 
• The plant was initially designed with an annual capacity of **1 million tonnes** of crude steel, which was later expanded in various phases.
 
• It serves as a critical industrial hub in **Eastern India**, contributing significantly to the production of railway materials like **wheels and axles**, as well as structural steel.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Second Five Year Plan (1956-1961)**:

 
 
• This plan was based on the **P.C. Mahalanobis Model**, which emphasized **rapid industrialization** with a focus on heavy industries.
 
• Under this plan, three major integrated steel plants were established in the public sector with foreign collaboration: **Bhilai**, **Rourkela**, and **Durgapur**.
 
 
 
• **Bhilai Steel Plant**:
 
 
• Located in **Bhilai**, **Chhattisgarh**, it was set up in **1955** with the collaboration of the **Soviet Union** (now **Russia**).
 
• It is an **eleven-time winner** of the Prime Minister's Trophy for the best integrated steel plant in the country.
 
 
 
• **Rourkela Steel Plant (RSP)**:
 
 
• Located in **Odisha**, it was the first integrated steel plant in the public sector in India, set up in **1959**.
 
• It was established in collaboration with **German** firms, specifically **Krupp** and **Demag**.
 
 
 
• **Bokaro Steel Plant**:
 
 
• Located in **Bokaro**, **Jharkhand**, it was the fourth integrated public sector steel plant in India.
 
• It was established in **1964** with the assistance of the **Soviet Union** during the **Third Five Year Plan**.
 
 
 
• **Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL)**:
 
 
• **SAIL** is a government-owned steel producer headquartered in **New Delhi**.
 
• It was incorporated in **1973** and currently holds the status of a **Maharatna** Central Public Sector Enterprise.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT the division of the Himalaya?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Aravali**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Himadri**, also known as the **Great Himalayas** or **Inner Himalayas**, is the northernmost and most continuous range of the **Himalayan** mountain system. It contains the highest peaks in the world, such as **Mount Everest** and **Kanchenjunga**, with an average elevation of **6,000 meters**.
 
• **Himachal**, or the **Lesser Himalayas**, lies to the south of the **Himadri**. This range is mainly composed of highly compressed and altered rocks, with an altitude varying between **3,700 and 4,500 meters**. It is famous for its hill stations like **Shimla**, **Mussoorie**, and **Nainital**.
 
• **Shiwalik** is the outermost range of the **Himalayas**. It extends over a width of **10-50 km** and has an altitude varying between **900 and 1,100 meters**. These ranges are composed of unconsolidated sediments brought down by rivers from the main **Himalayan** ranges located farther north.
 
• **Aravali** is one of the **oldest fold mountain ranges** in the world and is located in the western part of **India**, primarily in **Rajasthan**. It is not part of the **Himalayan** mountain system, which is a much younger geological formation. ***Hence, Aravali is NOT a division of the Himalaya.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Himalayan Mountain System:**

 
 
• The **Himalayas** are geologically **young and structurally fold mountains** that stretch across the northern borders of **India**.
 
• They run in a **west-east direction** from the **Indus River** to the **Brahmaputra River**, covering a distance of about **2,400 km**.
 
• The width of the **Himalayas** varies from **400 km** in **Kashmir** to **150 km** in **Arunachal Pradesh**.
 
 
 
• **Aravali Range:**
 
 
• The **Aravali Range** dates back to the **Proterozoic Era**, making it significantly older than the **Himalayas**, which were formed during the **Tertiary Period**.
 
• It spans approximately **692 km**, starting from **Gujarat**, passing through **Rajasthan** and **Haryana**, and ending in **Delhi**.
 
• The highest peak of the **Aravali Range** is **Guru Shikhar**, located on **Mount Abu**, with an elevation of **1,722 meters**.
 
• The range serves as a barrier preventing the eastward expansion of the **Thar Desert**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Longitudinal Valleys (Duns):** The longitudinal valleys lying between the **Lesser Himalayas (Himachal)** and the **Shiwaliks** are known as **Duns**. Well-known examples include **Dehra Dun**, **Kotli Dun**, and **Patli Dun**.
 
• **Trans-Himalayas:** Located immediately north of the **Great Himalayan** range, this region includes the **Karakoram**, **Ladakh**, and **Zanskar** ranges. It is also known as the **Tethys Himalayas**.
 
• **Regional Divisions:** Apart from longitudinal divisions, the **Himalayas** are also divided from west to east:
 
 
• **Punjab Himalayas** (between **Indus** and **Sutlej**).
 
• **Kumaon Himalayas** (between **Sutlej** and **Kali**).
 
• **Nepal Himalayas** (between **Kali** and **Teesta**).
 
• **Assam Himalayas** (between **Teesta** and **Dihang**).

questions.question: Which metal was unknown to the Harappan people?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Iron**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Harappan Civilization**, also known as the **Indus Valley Civilization (IVC)**, belonged to the **Bronze Age** (circa **3300 BCE to 1300 BCE**).
 
• While the Harappans were highly advanced in metallurgy, **Iron** was **unknown** to them. The use of iron in the Indian subcontinent began much later, during the **Vedic Period** around **1000 BCE**. ***Hence, option 1 is the correct answer.***
 
• Archaeological excavations at major sites like **Harappa**, **Mohenjo-daro**, and **Lothal** have revealed a wide variety of artifacts made of **Copper**, **Bronze**, **Gold**, and **Silver**, but no iron implements have been discovered.
 
• The **Harappans** produced **Bronze** by mixing **Copper** with **Tin**. Copper was sourced from the **Khetri mines** in **Rajasthan**, while **Tin** was likely imported from **Afghanistan**.
 
• The absence of **Iron** suggests that the Harappans relied on softer metals and stone tools for agriculture, construction, and warfare.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Use of Copper and Bronze:**

 
 
• **Copper** was the first metal to be used extensively by the Harappan people. They manufactured tools like **axes**, **saws**, **knives**, and **spearheads**.
 
• The invention of **Bronze** allowed for the creation of more durable tools and artistic figures, marking a significant technological leap.
 
 
 
• **Precious Metals (Gold and Silver):**
 
 
• **Gold** was used to create elaborate **jewelry**, including necklaces, bangles, and earrings. It is believed to have been sourced from **Southern India** (modern-day **Karnataka**) and **Afghanistan**.
 
• **Silver** was also widely used for making vessels and ornaments. The Harappans were among the earliest people in the world to use silver.
 
 
 
• **Lead and Tin:**
 
 
• The Harappans were aware of **Lead** and **Antimony**. **Tin** was a rare commodity and its scarcity is reflected in the limited number of high-quality bronze artifacts compared to copper ones.
 
 
 
• **Trade and Metallurgy:**
 
 
• The civilization maintained active trade links with **Mesopotamia** (modern-day **Iraq**) and **Oman**, exchanging metal goods for other commodities.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Technological Limitations:** Smelting **Iron** requires a much higher temperature (approx **1538°C**) compared to **Copper** (approx **1085°C**). The Harappans had not yet developed the advanced furnace technology required to extract iron from its ore.
 
• **Lost-Wax Technique:** One of the most famous metal artifacts of this era is the **"Dancing Girl"** statue found at **Mohenjo-daro**, created using the **Cire Perdue** or **lost-wax casting** method.
 
• **Transition to Iron Age:** The **Iron Age** in India is associated with the **Painted Grey Ware (PGW)** culture. Early evidence of iron usage has been found at sites like **Atranjikhera** in **Uttar Pradesh**, dating back to approximately **1000 BCE**, which is long after the decline of the mature Harappan phase.
 
• **Agricultural Implements:** Due to the lack of **Iron**, Harappan farmers used **wooden plows** and copper/bronze sickles for harvesting crops like **wheat** and **barley**.

questions.question: How do plants primarily get rid of excess water?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**By transpiration**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Transpiration** is the biological process through which plants eliminate **excess water** in the form of **water vapor** from their aerial parts, primarily the **leaves**.
 
• Approximately **97-99%** of the water absorbed by a plant's **roots** is not utilized for growth or **photosynthesis** but is instead released into the **atmosphere** via this process.
 
• This process mainly occurs through microscopic pores called **stomata**, which are located on the underside of the **leaves** and are regulated by **guard cells**.
 
• **Transpiration** serves several vital **functions**, including the creation of a **transpirational pull** (suction force) that aids in the upward transport of water and **minerals** from the **soil** to the top of the plant.
 
• It also helps in **thermoregulation**, providing a **cooling effect** to the plant during hot **weather**, similar to sweating in **humans**.
 
• *Hence, the correct option is By transpiration.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Transpiration**:

 
 
• **Stomatal Transpiration**: This is the most common type, accounting for about **80-90%** of the total water loss through **stomata**.
 
• **Cuticular Transpiration**: Occurs through the **cuticle** (waxy layer) of the **leaf**, contributing to about **5-10%** of water loss.
 
• **Lenticular Transpiration**: Water loss that happens through **lenticels**, which are small openings in the **bark** of woody **stems**.
 
 
 
• **Factors Affecting Rate**:
 
 
• **Light**: Increases the rate as **stomata** open in the presence of **sunlight**.
 
• **Temperature**: A higher **temperature** increases the rate of evaporation, thereby increasing **transpiration**.
 
• **Humidity**: If atmospheric **humidity** is high, the rate of **transpiration** decreases because the air is already saturated with **moisture**.
 
• **Wind Speed**: Moving air removes **water vapor** from the **leaf** surface, increasing the rate.
 
 
 
• **Guttation**: This is another method of water loss where water is released in **liquid droplets** from the edges of **leaves** through specialized structures called **hydathodes**. It usually occurs at **night** or early **morning** when **soil moisture** is high and **transpiration** is low.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Xylem**: This is the specialized **vascular tissue** responsible for the conduction of water and **nutrients** from the **roots** to the rest of the **plant**.
 
• **Cohesion-Tension Theory**: This **scientific theory** explains how water moves upwards against **gravity**. It relies on the **cohesive** forces between water molecules and the **tension** created by **transpiration** in the **leaves**.
 
• **Potometer**: A **laboratory instrument** used by **botanists** to measure the rate of **transpiration** in a plant shoot.
 
• **Adaptations**: **Xerophytes** (plants in dry climates, like **cacti**) have adapted features such as sunken **stomata**, thick **cuticles**, or leaves modified into **spines** to minimize **water loss**.
 
• **Environmental Impact**: **Transpiration** is a key component of the **water cycle**, as it contributes significantly to **atmospheric moisture** and **rainfall** patterns.

questions.question:
Which of the following statement regarding the fundamental rights of the Indian constitution is correct?

I. Article 26 is related Freedom from Taxation for Promotion of a Religion

II. Article 27 is related to freedom to manage religious affairs.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Neither I Nor II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 26** of the **Indian Constitution** provides the **freedom to manage religious affairs**. It states that every religious denomination has the right to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes, manage its own affairs in matters of religion, and own and acquire movable and immovable property. ***Hence, statement I is incorrect.***
 
• **Article 27** of the **Constitution** relates to the **freedom as to payment of taxes for promotion of any particular religion**. It mandates that no person shall be compelled to pay any taxes, the proceeds of which are specifically used for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion or religious denomination. ***Hence, statement II is incorrect.***
 
• Both articles are part of the **Right to Freedom of Religion**, which is a **Fundamental Right** guaranteed under **Part III** of the **Constitution of India**.
 
• The statements provided in the question have swapped the definitions of the two articles, making both descriptions factually wrong in the context of the **Article numbers** mentioned.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Neither I Nor II.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25–28):**

 
 
• **Article 25:** Guarantees freedom of **conscience** and the right to freely **profess, practice, and propagate** religion to all citizens. This right is subject to **public order, morality, and health**.
 
• **Article 26:** Protects collective religious rights. It allows **religious denominations** to manage their own internal affairs without state interference, provided they do not violate public order.
 
• **Article 27:** Prevents the **State** from using **taxpayer money** to favor one religion over another, upholding the **secular character** of the Indian polity.
 
• **Article 28:** Prohibits **religious instruction** in educational institutions wholly maintained out of **State funds**. In other institutions recognized by the State or receiving aid, religious instruction is permitted only with the **consent** of the individual (or guardian).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Difference between Tax and Fee:**

 
 
• Under **Article 27**, the **State** is prohibited from levying a **tax** for religious promotion. However, the courts have clarified that the **State can levy a fee** to provide secular services, such as providing **safety, health, and sanitation** facilities for pilgrims during festivals or at religious sites.
 
 
 
• **Religious Denominations:**
 
 
• For a group to be considered a **religious denomination** under **Article 26**, it must be a collection of individuals who have a **system of beliefs** (doctrines) which they regard as conducive to their spiritual well-being, a common **organization**, and a **distinctive name**.
 
 
 
• **Secularism in India:**
 
 
• The inclusion of these articles reinforces the **Positive Concept of Secularism** in **India**, where the State maintains an **equal distance** from all religions and gives equal respect to all faiths, rather than a total separation of state and religion seen in Western models.

questions.question: 'Chawng Laizawn' is a popular dance of which of the following Indian state/ Union Territory?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mizoram**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chawng Laizawn** is a popular and vibrant folk dance that originates from the **North-Eastern** state of **Mizoram**.
 
• This dance is specifically associated with the **Pawi** community, also known as the **Lai** tribe, who primarily inhabit the **Lawngtlai** district of **Mizoram**.
 
• The dance is traditionally performed on two distinct occasions: to celebrate a **successful hunt** (specifically when a warrior/hunter returns with a trophy) or during the **Pawl Kut** festival, which is a post-harvest festival.
 
• It is a rhythmic performance where **drums** and **gongs** serve as the primary musical instruments to provide the beat.
 
• The performance involves a group of dancers, often both men and women, who move in a **synchronized** and **circular fashion**, reflecting the cultural heritage and social cohesion of the **Mizo** people.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mizoram:**

 
 
• The state is famous for the **Cheraw Dance**, popularly known as the **Bamboo Dance**, where dancers move between horizontally placed bamboo poles.
 
• Other prominent folk dances of **Mizoram** include **Khuallam** (dance of the guests), **Chheihlam**, and **Sarlamkai** (a warrior dance).
 
• The major festivals of the state are known as **Kuts**, such as **Chapchar Kut** (celebrated in **March**), **Mim Kut**, and **Pawl Kut**.
 
 
 
• **Assam:**
 
 
• The most famous dance is **Bihu**, performed during the three Bihu festivals (**Rongali, Kongali, and Bhogali**).
 
• **Sattriya** is a **Classical Dance** of India that originated in the **Sattras** (monasteries) of **Assam**, founded by the saint **Srimanta Sankardev** in the **15th century**.
 
• Other folk dances include **Bagurumba** (performed by the **Bodo** community) and **Jhumur**.
 
 
 
• **Ladakh:**
 
 
• **Shondol** is known as the '**Royal Dance**' of **Ladakh** and was historically performed for the **King of Ladakh** on special occasions.
 
• **Jabro** is a traditional folk dance of the **Nomadic** people of the **Tibetan** plateau living in the **Changthang** region of **Ladakh**.
 
 
 
• **Chhattisgarh:**
 
 
• **Panthi** is a famous folk dance of the **Satnami** community, performed on the birth anniversary of **Guru Ghasidas**.
 
• **Raut Nacha** is a traditional dance performed by the **Yaduvanshi** (cowherds) community, typically during the **Dev Uthani Ekadashi** festival.
 
• **Karma** dance is another significant folk dance performed by tribal groups like the **Gonds**, **Baigas**, and **Oraons**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Cultural Significance:** In **Mizo** culture, dances are not merely for entertainment but are deeply intertwined with **rituals** and **community milestones**.
 
• **Lai Tribe:** The **Lai** people have a distinct dialect and cultural practices within the broader **Mizo** identity, and **Chawng Laizawn** is a key marker of their specific ethnic pride.
 
• **Instruments:** Traditional **Mizo** music heavily relies on percussion. The **Khuang** (drum) is considered the most important instrument and is used in almost all folk dances.
 
• **Mizoram Statehood:** **Mizoram** became the **23rd state** of the **Indian Union** on **20 February 1987**, following the **Mizo Accord** of **1986**.

questions.question: Which Indian state is famous for the folk dance called 'Kajri'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Uttar Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kajri** is one of the most prominent folk song and dance genres of **India**, predominantly famous in the state of **Uttar Pradesh** and some parts of **Bihar**.
 
• It is traditionally associated with the **monsoon season**, specifically the months of **Shravan** and **Bhadrapada** (typically **July**, **August**, and **September**), when the dark clouds bring relief from the summer heat.
 
• The origin of **Kajri** is believed to be the city of **Mirzapur** in **Eastern Uttar Pradesh**. Legend suggests it evolved from the longing of a woman for her husband during the rainy season.
 
• The performance of **Kajri** is a vital part of the **Teej festival**, where women gather, sing, and dance while enjoying swings in the rain.
 
• It is usually sung in the **Bhojpuri** and **Maithili** dialects, reflecting the local culture and rural lifestyle of the **Gangetic plains**. ***Hence, the correct answer is Uttar Pradesh.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Assam:**

 
 
• This state is world-famous for the **Bihu** dance, which is performed during the three **Bihu festivals**: **Rongali Bihu**, **Kongali Bihu**, and **Bhogali Bihu**.
 
• Another significant dance is **Sattriya**, which is one of the eight **Classical Dances of India**, introduced by the great saint **Srimanta Sankardev** in the **15th century**.
 
• Other folk forms include **Bagurumba** (of the **Bodo** community) and **Ojapali**.
 
 
 
• **Punjab:**
 
 
• **Punjab** is renowned for its high-energy folk dances such as **Bhangra**, traditionally performed by men during the harvest festival of **Vaisakhi**.
 
• **Giddha** is the female counterpart to **Bhangra**, characterized by rhythmic clapping and singing of folk verses called **Boliyan**.
 
• Other traditional dances include **Jhumar**, **Luddi**, and **Sammi**, reflecting the agrarian life of the **Five Rivers** region.
 
 
 
• **Maharashtra:**
 
 
• The most iconic folk dance of **Maharashtra** is **Lavani**, which combines powerful rhythm, traditional **Dholak** beats, and expressive lyrics.
 
• The **Koli** dance is performed by the fishing community, mimicking the movement of waves and the casting of nets.
 
• Other notable forms include **Dhangari Gaja** (shepherd dance), **Lezim**, and **Povada**, which is a narrative song form praising historical heroes like **Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj**.
 
 
 
• **Uttar Pradesh (Other Dances):**
 
 
• Apart from **Kajri**, the state is the cradle of **Kathak**, a major **Classical Indian Dance** form.
 
• Folk forms like **Charkula** (popular in the **Braj** region), **Raslila** (depicting the life of **Lord Krishna**), and **Nautanki** (a form of folk theater) are widely practiced across the state.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• In the **Gregorian calendar**, this auspicious day typically falls in the month of **June**, though occasionally it may begin in late **May** depending on the lunar cycle.

• **Prominent Locations**: The festival is celebrated with immense fervor at the **Ghats** of the **Ganga** in holy cities such as **Varanasi**, **Haridwar**, **Rishikesh**, **Prayagraj**, and **Garhmukteshwar**. Devotees gather in **thousands** to take a ritualistic **holy dip** in the waters.

questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The unit **kJ** represents a **kilojoule**, which is a multiple of the base unit of energy, the **joule (J)**.
 
• In the **International System of Units (SI)**, the prefix **kilo-** is used to denote a factor of **10³** or **1000**.
 
• The **joule** is defined as the amount of **energy transferred** to an object when a force of **one newton** acts on that object in the direction of the force's motion through a distance of **one meter**.
 
• Mathematically, the relationship is defined as **1 kilojoule = 1000 joules**. This conversion is fundamental in **thermodynamics**, **physics**, and **chemistry** when measuring heat or work.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Metric System Multiples**:

 
 
• **Mega (M)**: Represents **10⁶** or **1,000,000** units. Therefore, **1 MJ = 1,000,000 J**.
 
• **Giga (G)**: Represents **10⁹** or **1,000,000,000** units.
 
• **Milli (m)**: Represents **10−³** or **1/1000** of a unit. Therefore, **1 mJ = 0.001 J**.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context**:
 
 
• The unit is named after the English physicist **James Prescott Joule**, who demonstrated the **mechanical equivalent of heat** in the **19th century**.
 
 
 
• **Energy Conversions**:
 
 
• **1 calorie (cal)** is equivalent to approximately **4.184 joules**.
 
• **1 kilowatt-hour (kWh)**, often used for electrical energy billing, is equal to **3,600,000 joules** or **3600 kJ**.
 
• The **joule** can also be expressed in terms of other SI units as **1 kg·m²/s²** or **1 Watt-second**.

questions.question: In the context of population change, if the birth rate is ______ than death rate, the population will ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**less, decrease**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Population change** refers to the change in the **number of people** during a **specific time** period. This is a dynamic process influenced by three main factors: **births**, **deaths**, and **migration**.
 
• The **Birth rate** is the number of **live births per 1,000 people** in a year, while the **Death rate** is the number of **deaths per 1,000 people** in a year.
 
• When the **birth rate is less than the death rate**, it signifies that the number of people dying exceeds the number of babies being born. As a result, the **total population will decrease** over that period, assuming no significant inward migration. ***Hence, the statement aligns with the logic of natural decrease.***
 
• The difference between the **birth rate** and the **death rate** of a country is called the **natural growth rate**. If the death rate is higher, the natural growth rate becomes **negative**.
 
• Until the **1800s**, the world's population grew steadily but slowly because, although many babies were born (high birth rate), the death rate was also high due to poor **health facilities** and **food shortages**.
 
• In modern times, many developed nations have seen a **population decline** because their **birth rate** has fallen **below** the **death rate**, a phenomenon often observed in countries with aging populations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Components of Population Change:**

 
 
• There are three primary components: **Births**, **Deaths**, and **Migration**. While births and deaths are **natural causes**, migration is a **man-made** or induced cause of change.
 
• **Natural Increase** occurs when the **birth rate** is **higher** than the **death rate**. This was the primary reason for the **population explosion** in the **20th century**.
 
 
 
• **Migration Dynamics:**
 
 
• **Migration** is the movement of people across **boundaries**. It can be **internal** (within the country) or **international** (between countries).
 
• **Immigration** is when a person **arrives** in a new country, increasing its population, while **Emigration** is when a person **leaves** a country, decreasing its population.
 
• Countries like the **United States of America** and **Australia** have gained in-numbers by **in-migration** or **immigration**.
 
 
 
• **Demographic Transition:**
 
 
• This is a model used to represent the transition from **high birth and death rates** to **low birth and death rates** as a country develops from a **pre-industrial** to an **industrialized** economic system.
 
• In the **final stage** of demographic transition, both birth and death rates decline significantly, often leading to a **stable** or **declining population**.
 
 
 
• **Factors Influencing Rates:**
 
 
• **Birth rates** are influenced by **social factors**, **education levels** (especially of women), and **economic stability**.
 
• **Death rates** have plummeted globally due to **advancements in medicine**, **better sanitation**, and **improved nutrition**.
 
• The **World Population** reached **8 billion** in **November 2022**, largely driven by high natural increase in **developing regions**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Statistical Facts:**

 
 
• A **stationary population** occurs when the **birth rate** is exactly **equal** to the **death rate** and there is no net migration.
 
• The **Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)** and **Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR)** are critical subsets of the death rate that reflect the **socio-economic development** and **healthcare quality** of a nation.
 
• The **Replacement Level Fertility** is the total fertility rate—the average number of children born per woman—at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next, without migration. This value is roughly **2.1** in most countries.

questions.question: Which of the following economic activity is NOT included in the primary sector?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Manufacturing**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Primary Sector** of the economy includes all those activities the end purpose of which consists of exploiting **natural resources**. It forms the base for all other products that we subsequently make.
 
• **Fishing** is a primary activity because it involves the direct extraction of **aquatic resources** from nature without significant chemical or mechanical transformation at the point of harvest. ***Hence, it is included in the primary sector.***
 
• **Mining** involves the extraction of minerals and ores directly from the **earth's crust**. Since it deals with raw earth materials, it is classified under the primary sector. ***Hence, it is included in the primary sector.***
 
• **Forestry** involves activities such as logging, timber production, and the collection of wild-grown forest products. It relies entirely on the **biological and environmental** growth of forests. ***Hence, it is included in the primary sector.***
 
• **Manufacturing** refers to the process of converting raw materials into **finished goods** using machinery, tools, and labor. This activity adds value to primary products and is categorized under the **Secondary Sector**. ***Hence, statement 3 is not included in the primary sector and is the correct answer.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sectors of Economy:**

 
 
• **Primary Sector:** This sector is also known as the **Agriculture and Related Sector**. It includes **Agriculture**, **Dairy**, **Fishing**, **Forestry**, and **Mining**. In developing countries like **India**, it remains a significant provider of **employment**.
 
• **Secondary Sector:** This sector covers activities in which natural products are changed into other forms through ways of **manufacturing**. It is also called the **Industrial Sector**. Examples include **Textile mills**, **Steel plants**, and **Automobile assembly**.
 
• **Tertiary Sector:** Often called the **Service Sector**, it provides support to the primary and secondary sectors. It includes **Transport**, **Banking**, **Insurance**, **Education**, and **Health Services**. It currently contributes the highest share to India's **GDP**.
 
 
 
• **Advanced Classifications:**
 
 
• **Quaternary Sector:** This is a knowledge-based part of the economy, including services such as **Information Technology (IT)**, **Research and Development (R&D)**, and **Financial planning**.
 
• **Quinary Sector:** This includes the highest level of decision-making in a society or economy. This includes top officials in **Government**, **Science**, and **Universities**.
 
 
 
• **Indian Context:**
 
 
• In **India**, while the primary sector employs nearly **45-50%** of the workforce, its contribution to the **Gross Value Added (GVA)** is relatively lower compared to the service sector, highlighting the issue of **disguised unemployment** in rural areas.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• Workers in the primary sector are often called **Red-collar workers** due to the outdoor nature of their work.
 
• Workers in the secondary sector (specifically physical labor) are known as **Blue-collar workers**.
 
• The transition of an economy from primary to secondary and then to tertiary is known as **Structural Transformation**. In **India**, there has been a direct jump from the primary to the tertiary sector in terms of **GDP share**, bypassing a dominant manufacturing phase.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Literary Context**: **Preeti Shenoy's** writing style is frequently categorized as **popular fiction** or **commercial fiction**, making it highly accessible to a broad audience in India.

questions.question: Which of the following sector is NOT covered under Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Leather Industry**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme** was launched by the **Government of India** to boost **domestic manufacturing**, increase **exports**, and make India a global supply chain hub under the **Atmanirbhar Bharat** initiative.
 
• The scheme initially targeted three industries in **March 2020** but was later expanded to cover **14 key sectors** with a total outlay of approximately **₹1.97 lakh crore**.
 
• **Manufacturing of Medical Devices** is a recognized sector under the PLI scheme, specifically aimed at reducing import dependence on high-end medical equipment like **radiology and imaging devices**, **anaesthetics**, and **cancer care equipment**. ***Hence, statement 1 is covered under the scheme.***
 
• **Automobiles and Auto Components** were included in the scheme in **September 2021** with a financial outlay of **₹25,938 crore** to incentivize the production of **Advanced Automotive Technology (AAT)** products and **Electric Vehicles (EVs)**. ***Hence, statement 3 is covered under the scheme.***
 
• **Drones and Drone Components** were approved under the PLI scheme in **2021** to position India as a global drone hub by **2030**, providing an incentive of **20%** of the value addition made by the manufacturer. ***Hence, statement 4 is covered under the scheme.***
 
• The **Leather Industry** is **not** one of the 14 sectors currently covered under the **PLI scheme**. While the government supports this sector through the **Indian Footwear and Leather Development Programme (IFLDP)**, it does not fall under the specific PLI framework. ***Hence, the Leather Industry is the correct answer.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **List of 14 Sectors:** The 14 sectors under the PLI scheme include **Mobile Manufacturing**, **Medical Devices**, **Critical Key Starting Materials (KSMs)/Drug Intermediaries**, **Automobiles and Auto Components**, **Pharmaceutical Drugs**, **Specialty Steel**, **Telecom and Networking Products**, **Electronic/Technology Products**, **White Goods (ACs and LEDs)**, **Food Products**, **Textile Products (MMF segment and Technical Textiles)**, **High-Efficiency Solar PV Modules**, **Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery**, and **Drones**.
 
• **Objectives:** The primary goal is to provide **financial incentives** to companies based on their **incremental sales** from products manufactured in domestic units, encouraging **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)** and large-scale manufacturing.
 
• **Implementation:** Different ministries manage specific sectors. For example, the **Ministry of Heavy Industries** oversees Automobiles and Drones, while the **Department of Pharmaceuticals** manages Medical Devices and Drugs.
 
• **Economic Impact:** The scheme is expected to contribute significantly to India's **GDP**, create **employment opportunities** for millions, and significantly reduce the trade deficit by promoting **import substitution**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Tenure:** The duration of the PLI schemes varies by sector, typically ranging from **4 to 6 years**, starting from the base year **2019-20** or **2021-22**.
 
• **Eligibility:** Incentives are provided to both **MSMEs** and **Large Enterprises** that meet specific investment and production thresholds defined for each category.
 
• **Recent Developments:** In **2023**, the government considered expanding the PLI to other sectors like **Toys** and **Bicycles**, but as of the current official list, the **Leather Industry** remains excluded from the PLI umbrella.

questions.question:
Which of the following is a type of service in volleyball?

I. Jump and Serve

II. Floating serve
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **service** in **volleyball** is the act of putting the ball into play by the **right-back player**, placed in the **service zone**. It is the only technical action where a player has total control over the ball without interference from teammates or opponents.
 
• **Jump Serve (Jump and Serve)**: This is an advanced type of serve where the player increases the **power** and **height** of the serve by jumping to hit the ball. The server tosses the ball high, takes a rhythmic approach, and strikes the ball in mid-air. This technique generates high **velocity** and a steep downward angle, making it difficult for the receiving team to pass. *Hence, statement I is correct.*
 
• **Floating Serve (Floater)**: A **floating serve** is hit with very little to no **spin**. Because of the lack of rotation, the ball's path becomes **unpredictable** as it interacts with the air currents, causing it to "dance" or move suddenly to the left, right, or drop down. This makes it extremely challenging for the **defensive players** to track and handle accurately. *Hence, statement II is correct.*
 
• Both the **Jump Serve** and the **Floating Serve** are fundamental strategies used in modern competitive volleyball to gain an advantage right from the start of the **rally**.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Both I and II.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **History of Volleyball:**

 
 
• Volleyball was invented in **1895** by **William G. Morgan**, a physical education director at the **YMCA** in **Holyoke, Massachusetts**. It was originally called "**Mintonette**" and was designed as an indoor sport for businessmen who found basketball too vigorous.
 
• The game was added to the **Olympic Games** program for the first time during the **1964 Tokyo Olympics**.
 
 
 
• **Basic Rules and Court Dimensions:**
 
 
• A standard **volleyball court** measures **18 meters** in length and **9 meters** in width. It is divided by a net into two **9m x 9m** halves.
 
• The height of the net is **2.43 meters** for **men** and **2.24 meters** for **women**.
 
• Each team consists of **6 players** on the court. A team is allowed a maximum of **three hits** to return the ball over the net.
 
 
 
• **Common Volleyball Terminology:**
 
 
• **Ace**: A serve that results directly in a point because it hits the floor untouched or the receiving team cannot keep it in play.
 
• **Libero**: A specialized **defensive player** who wears a different colored jersey and can substitute for any back-row player without notice to the officials.
 
• **Dig**: The act of preventing the ball from hitting the floor after an attack or spike by the opponent.
 
• **Set**: A tactical pass, usually the second contact, that directs the ball towards a hitter to **spike** it into the opponent's court.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Governing Body:** The **Fédération Internationale de Volleyball (FIVB)** is the international governing body for all forms of volleyball. It was founded in **1947** and is headquartered in **Lausanne, Switzerland**.
 
• **Variations of Serves:** Besides jump and floating serves, players also utilize the **Underhand Serve** (often for beginners), the **Overhand Serve**, and the **Topspin Serve** (which rotates forward rapidly to drop quickly into the court).
 
• **Scoring System:** Modern volleyball uses the **Rally Point System**, where a point is scored on every single rally, regardless of which team is serving. Matches are typically played as the **best of five sets**, with the first four sets played to **25 points** and the fifth set (if necessary) played to **15 points**.

questions.question: How many distinct temples are there in the Dilwara Temples complex?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**5**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Dilwara Temples** are a world-famous group of **Svetambara Jain temples** located about 2.5 kilometers from the **Mount Abu** hill station, the only hill station in **Rajasthan**.
 
• There are **5** distinct temples in the complex, each dedicated to a different **Jain Tirthankara** and possessing its own unique architectural identity.
 
• These temples were built between the **11th and 16th centuries** (specifically between **1031 AD and 1582 AD**) during the reign of the **Chaulukya dynasty** (Solanki rulers).
 
• The complex is globally renowned for its extraordinary **architecture** and stunning **marble stone carvings**, often considered superior to the Taj Mahal in terms of intricate detailing.
 
• The five temples included in the complex are **Vimal Vasahi**, **Luna Vasahi**, **Pittalhar**, **Parshvanath**, and **Mahavir Swami**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Vimal Vasahi Temple:**

 
 
• Built in **1031 AD** by **Vimal Shah**, a minister of the **Solanki King Bhimdev I**.
 
• It is dedicated to the **first Jain Tirthankara**, **Lord Rishabha** (also known as Adinath).
 
• The temple is famous for its "**Rang Mandap**," a central hall supported by **12 decorated pillars** and a magnificent carved dome.
 
 
 
• **Luna Vasahi Temple:**
 
 
• Constructed in **1230 AD** by two brothers, **Vastupal and Tejpal**, who were ministers of **Raja Vir Dhawal** of Gujarat.
 
• It is dedicated to the **22nd Tirthankara**, **Lord Neminatha**.
 
• The temple is noted for its "**Hathishala**" (elephant cell), featuring **10 marble elephants**, and its incredibly delicate pendant carvings in the central dome.
 
 
 
• **Pittalhar Temple:**
 
 
• This temple was built by **Bhima Shah**, another minister from Gujarat, during the **14th-15th century**.
 
• It is dedicated to **Lord Adinath** and houses a massive statue of the deity cast in **five metals** (Panchaloha), with **brass (Pittal)** being the dominant metal, giving the temple its name.
 
 
 
• **Parshvanath Temple (Khartar Vasahi):**
 
 
• Built between **1458 and 1459** by the **Mandlika** family, it is the tallest shrine in the Dilwara complex.
 
• It is dedicated to the **23rd Tirthankara**, **Lord Parshvanath**, and consists of a **three-story** building with grey stone carvings on the exterior walls.
 
 
 
• **Mahavir Swami Temple:**
 
 
• Completed in **1582**, it is the smallest and newest temple in the complex, dedicated to the **24th and last Tirthankara**, **Lord Mahavira**.
 
• Despite its small size, it features beautiful **wall paintings** on the upper walls of the porch, dating back to **1764**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Architectural Style:** The temples are built in the **Maru-Gurjara** style of architecture, which originated in **Western India**. This style is characterized by **ornate carvings**, **multiple shrines**, and **vaulted ceilings**.
 
• **Material Sourcing:** The **white marble** used for the construction was transported from the **Arasuri hills** near **Ambaji** in Gujarat, which was a massive logistical feat at the time.
 
• **Location:** Situated at a high altitude in the **Aravalli Range**, the site provides a serene environment conducive to **meditation** and religious activities.
 
• **Preservation:** The complex is managed by the **Seth Kalyanji Paramanandji Pedhi** trust and remains a vital **pilgrimage site** for the Jain community worldwide.

questions.question: What is molecular mass?

options.text: The total number of atoms in a molecule
The sum of the valencies of the atoms in a molecule
The sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule
The volume occupied by a molecule

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **molecular mass** of a substance is defined as the **sum of the atomic masses** of all the atoms present in a single molecule of that substance. ***Hence, option 3 is correct.***
 
• It is the **relative mass** of a molecule compared to **1/12th** of the mass of one **carbon-12** atom.
 
• Calculation Method: To find the molecular mass, we multiply the **atomic mass** of each element by the number of its atoms in the chemical formula and then add the results. For example, in **Water (H2O)**, the mass is (**2 x 1u**) + (**1 x 16u**) = **18u**.
 
• The **total number of atoms** in a molecule is known as its **atomicity**, not its molecular mass. For instance, the atomicity of **Phosphorus (P4)** is **4**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• The **valency** of an atom is its combining capacity. The sum of valencies is used to determine chemical formulas but does not represent the mass of the molecule. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The **volume** occupied by a molecule relates to its physical state and conditions like **temperature** and **pressure**, as described by **Avogadro's Law**, rather than its mass. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Atomic Mass Unit (u)**: Also known as the **unified mass**, it is the standard unit used for expressing atomic and molecular weights. It is exactly **1/12th** the mass of an unbound neutral atom of **carbon-12** at rest and in its ground state.
 
• **Molar Mass**: While molecular mass refers to the mass of a single molecule (in **u**), **molar mass** refers to the mass of **one mole** of the substance (**6.022 x 10^23** molecules) and is expressed in **grams per mole (g/mol)**. Numerically, molecular mass and molar mass are the same.
 
• **Formula Unit Mass**: This term is specifically used for **ionic compounds** (like **NaCl** or **CaCl2**) where the constituent particles are ions rather than discrete molecules. It is calculated the same way as molecular mass.
 
• **Significance in Chemistry**: Molecular mass is essential for **stoichiometry** calculations in chemical reactions, allowing scientists to calculate the exact **proportions** of reactants needed to produce a specific amount of product.
 
• **Example Calculations**:
 
 
• **Carbon Dioxide (CO2)**: (**1 x 12u**) + (**2 x 16u**) = **44u**.
 
• **Methane (CH4)**: (**1 x 12u**) + (**4 x 1u**) = **16u**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Standard Reference**: The current scale for atomic and molecular masses is based on **Carbon-12**, adopted by the **IUPAC** in **1961** to replace older scales based on Oxygen.
 
• **Precision**: Molecular mass can be determined with high precision using **Mass Spectrometry**, which measures the **mass-to-charge ratio** of ionized molecules.
 
• **Dalton (Da)**: In biology and biochemistry, the unit **Dalton** is frequently used interchangeably with the unified atomic mass unit (**u**) to describe the mass of large organic molecules like **proteins** and **DNA**.
 
• **Gram Molecular Mass**: This is simply the molecular mass of a substance expressed in **grams**. For example, the gram molecular mass of **Oxygen (O2)** is **32g**.

questions.question:
Which of the following is correct regarding Gitam?

I. It is the simplest type of composition.

II. It is very simple in construction, with an easy and melodious flow of music.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the realm of **Indian Classical Music**, specifically the **Carnatic** tradition, **Gitam** (also spelled **Geetham**) is recognized as the **simplest type of musical composition**. It is designed primarily for students who have moved past basic exercises to understand the melodic structure of a **Raga**. *Hence, statement I is correct.*
 
• A **Gitam** is characterized by its **very simple construction**. Unlike more complex forms like **Kritis** or **Varnas**, it does not have distinct sections like **Pallavi**, **Anupallavi**, and **Charana**. Instead, it features a **continuous and melodious flow** of music. *Hence, statement II is correct.*
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Both I and II.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Structural Features of Gitam:**

 
 
• The term **Gitam** literally translates to "**song**." In these compositions, the **Sahitya** (lyrics) and the **Svara** (notes) are given equal importance. There are no **Sangatis** (variations) or complex **Gamaka** (ornamentations) used, making it easy for beginners to perform.
 
• It is typically set to **Madhyama Kala** (medium tempo). The **Sahitya** often consists of praises for **Gods** and **Goddesses**, reflecting the **Bhakti** (devotional) essence of **Indian music**.
 
 
 
• **Historical Significance:**
 
 
• **Purandara Dasa**, widely revered as the **Pitamaha** (grandfather) of **Carnatic music**, is credited with standardizing the teaching methodology, which includes the **Pillari Gitams**.
 
• The **Pillari Gitams** are usually the first few songs taught to students and are composed in praise of **Lord Ganesha**, such as the famous "**Sri Gananatha**" in **Raga Malahari**.
 
 
 
• **Types of Gitams:**
 
 
• **Samanya Gitam**: Also known as **Sanchari Gitam**, these are ordinary compositions where the **Sahitya** is religious or philosophical.
 
• **Lakshana Gitam**: These are unique because the **Sahitya** describes the **Lakshanas** (characteristics) of the **Raga** itself, including its **Arohana** (ascending scale), **Avarohana** (descending scale), and **Varjya** notes.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Musical Components:**

 
 
• **Tala**: Gitams are usually set to simple **Suladi Sapta Talas** like **Rupaka**, **Triputa**, **Dhruva**, and **Matya**.
 
• **Language**: The lyrics are commonly found in **Sanskrit**, **Kannada**, or a specialized musical dialect known as **Bhandira Bhasha**.
 
• **Pedagogical Role**: Learning **Gitams** is a crucial milestone for a student to grasp the **Svarupa** (personality) of different **Ragas** like **Kalyani**, **Sankarabharanam**, or **Mohanam** before advancing to the **Varnam** stage.

questions.question: EnviStats India 2025: Environment Statistics has been released by which of the following?

options.text: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **EnviStats India 2025: Environment Statistics** is a flagship publication released by the **National Statistical Office (NSO)**, which operates under the **Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI)** of the Government of India.
 
• The report provides comprehensive **data and statistics** related to the environment, including **physical assets**, **biodiversity**, **forests**, and **climate-related indicators** within the Indian territory.
 
• The publication follows the **System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA)** framework, which is the international statistical standard for environmental-economic accounting adopted by the **United Nations Statistical Commission** in **2012**.
 
• It aims to bridge the gap between **economic policy** and **environmental sustainability** by providing **quantitative data** that helps in assessing the impact of economic activities on natural resources.
 
• The **2025 edition** (and its predecessors) serves as a critical resource for monitoring **India’s progress** towards the **Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)**, particularly those concerning **Clean Water and Sanitation (SDG 6)**, **Climate Action (SDG 13)**, and **Life on Land (SDG 15)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation (MoSPI):**

 
 
• This **Ministry** was created as an independent entity on **15th October 1999** following the merger of the **Department of Statistics** and the **Department of Programme Implementation**.
 
• The **National Statistical Office (NSO)** under this ministry is responsible for the conduct of large-scale sample surveys and the **compilation of national accounts**, including the **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**.
 
 
 
• **System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA):**
 
 
• The **SEEA framework** integrates economic and environmental data to provide a **multipurpose information system** for understanding the interactions between the **economy and the environment**.
 
• It facilitates the calculation of **Green GDP**, which adjusts the traditional **GDP** by accounting for **environmental degradation** and **resource depletion**.
 
 
 
• **Other Ministries and their Roles:**
 
 
• The **Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC)** is the **nodal agency** for the planning, promotion, and coordination of **India's environmental and forestry programs**; however, the statistical compilation for **EnviStats** is handled by **MoSPI**.
 
• The **Ministry of Home Affairs** is primarily responsible for **internal security**, **border management**, and the **Census of India** (via the Registrar General).
 
• The **Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment** focuses on the **welfare and empowerment** of marginalized sections of society, such as **Scheduled Castes**, **OBCs**, and **persons with disabilities**.
 
 
 
• **Significance of EnviStats:**
 
 
• The report includes detailed accounts of **land cover**, **water use**, and **solid waste management** across different **Indian states and Union Territories**.
 
• By providing **time-series data**, it allows researchers to track **long-term environmental trends** and the efficiency of **government conservation schemes** like **Namami Gange** or the **National Afforestation Programme**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Global Context:** India is one of the few countries that have actively implemented the **SEEA framework** to produce **Environmental Accounts**, aligning its domestic statistical practices with **global benchmarks** set by the **United Nations**.
 
• **Data Sources:** The **MoSPI** collaborates with several technical agencies like the **Forest Survey of India (FSI)**, **Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)**, and **Central Ground Water Board (CGWB)** to collect primary data for these statistical volumes.
 
• **Scope:** **EnviStats India** is typically released in **two volumes**: Volume I focuses on **Environmental Statistics** (based on the **FDES 2013** framework), while Volume II focuses on **Environmental Accounts**.
